analysis.one_liner: Speeds federal pipeline permitting by weakening state water, environmental, and endangered-species reviews, and forces approval of the Mountain Valley Pipeline with no court challenges allowed.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House committees without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and Congress ended January 3, 2023 without acting on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite parts of the Clean Water Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and the Endangered Species Act to force faster approvals of oil and gas pipelines. It would set strict deadlines after which permits are automatically approved, narrow states' power to object under the Clean Water Act, shorten environmental reviews, and limit lawsuits. It also singles out one specific project — the Mountain Valley Pipeline in Virginia and West Virginia — and requires the government to issue every remaining permit within 21 days, with no court able to review that decision.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas pipeline developers, especially the Mountain Valley Pipeline project in Virginia and West Virginia, which Section 5 would force to completion within 21 days with no judicial review. Broader construction and energy firms also gain from shortened environmental reviews, automatic approval when agencies miss deadlines, shortened lawsuit windows, and a narrowed definition of protected waters. Landowners and communities along pipeline routes, people who drink from downstream waters, and endangered species lose the review and challenge rights the bill removes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pipeline developers and fossil fuel firms

how_it_helps.text: It sets hard deadlines for federal agencies: water-quality certifications must be completed within one year or waived, environmental reviews within two years, and endangered-species consultations shortened — after which approvals are treated as granted.
It narrows the scope of state Clean Water Act reviews to water-quality compliance only, limiting states' ability to block or condition energy projects.

It permanently reissues nationwide permit 12 for oil and gas pipelines, ratifies existing permits as having minimal environmental effects, and exempts the nationwide permit's reissuance from endangered-species consultation and NEPA review.
It requires federal agencies to issue all remaining permits for the Mountain Valley Pipeline within 21 days of enactment, and bars any court challenge to those approvals.

analysis.who_pays: State environmental agencies lose their say over pipeline water impacts; landowners and communities along routes lose their day in court; endangered species lose consultation protections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near pipelines and taxpayers' waters

drawbacks.text: By narrowing Clean Water Act section 401 so states may only consider whether the discharge meets water quality requirements, the bill would strip states of the ability to weigh broader water-resource impacts, and a missed one-year deadline would count as automatic approval.

Section 5 would approve the Mountain Valley Pipeline within 21 days, reissue its scientific approvals verbatim, preempt any conflicting law, and bar all judicial review — meaning affected landowners and states could not challenge the project in court.

The bill would shorten environmental impact statements to 150–300 pages with a 2-year deadline, shorten endangered-species consultations, and waive Endangered Species Act consultation entirely for reissuing the nationwide pipeline permit, reducing the scrutiny projects face.
It would limit the definition of protected 'waters of the United States' by excluding ephemeral streams, many wetlands, and groundwater — waters that feed drinking-water supplies downstream.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim — faster, more predictable federal permitting — addresses a real frustration for builders of all kinds, and its deadlines for agencies have a plausible rationale. But the way it pursued that goal was heavily weighted toward pipeline builders: it narrowed the scope of water-quality reviews, stripped endangered-species protections from nationwide pipeline permits, imposed a blanket 60-day limit on lawsuits over pipeline permits, and — most starkly — ordered approval of one company's pipeline within 21 days while barring any court from reviewing that decision. Those provisions trade away meaningful public safeguards for private construction timelines, without evidence in the record that the speed gained justifies the loss of review.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the House in December 2022 and referred to three committees, but no committee took it up and the House never voted on it; it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 1, 2022 and referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure, Natural Resources, and Agriculture committees.
Within two days it was routed to three subcommittees; no hearings, markups, or floor action ever followed.
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023, and the bill was never again introduced as written.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State water agencies, environmental groups, and landowners along the Mountain Valley Pipeline route benefit from the bill's death, since the legal tools it would have stripped away remain intact. Pipeline developers and the Mountain Valley Pipeline partnership lose the shortcut they sought.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no meaningful partisan or cross-party support was ever demonstrated.

industries.note: The bill would gut the main tools states and environmental groups use to challenge pipeline approvals, guarantee permits if agencies miss deadlines, and hand one company a congressionally mandated approval with no court review.

industries.industry: Mountain Valley Pipeline (Equinor and Consolidated Edison-backed JV partners)
industries.note: Section 5 would complete a specific half-built pipeline by statute within 21 days, overriding state, forest, and wildlife protections and barring judicial review — a direct transfer of a permitting dispute to a private beneficiary.
Their Clean Water Act certification authority would be narrowed to water-quality compliance alone, with deadlines that convert inaction into automatic approval.
Deadlines and page limits would speed permitting for projects of many kinds, not just pipelines, though the same limits apply to projects affecting their communities.
